items.q: An SLO of 99.9% over a 30-day window allows roughly how much downtime?
items.explain: 0.1% of 30 days is about 43 minutes. The error budget turns a percentage into a concrete allowance you can spend on risk.

items.q: Burn-rate alerting is valuable because it…
choices: Measures how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO window
items.explain: Burn rate is error rate divided by budgeted error rate: fast-burn alerts catch budget exhaustion hours before the window closes.

items.q: In an incident, the incident commander's job is to…
choices: Coordinate the response, hold the big picture, and authorize decisions
items.explain: The IC coordinates, tracks state, and unblocks. Specialists do the technical work; the IC keeps them pointed at the same problem.

choices: Proportion of requests served successfully within 300ms
items.explain: SLIs measure what users experience: the share of fast, successful requests. Fleet CPU is a cause, not a user experience.
Google's SRE framing: latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the minimum useful dashboard for any user-facing service.

choices: Systemic fixes: what the system allowed and how to change it
items.explain: Blameless reviews treat human error as a symptom of system design; the output is structural fixes, not punishment.

paths.il_provides: I'm your instructor for this path, and here's what I give you: the reliability spine every SRE interview runs on — SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets you can do on a whiteboard, incident command you can narrate minute by minute, observability you can design aloud, and capacity math with the cost of every nine stated. We close with six full design reps and a scored mock circuit, so you walk into the loop with the round shapes already automatic.

choices: Developers merge small changes to main frequently
items.explain: Small, frequent merges to trunk shrink merge conflicts and keep the pipeline testing the real codebase.

choices: Deploys to all servers at once
Releases to a small subset first, then expands on success
items.explain: Canary exposes a small population, watches metrics, then rolls forward: contained blast radius with real-user signal.

choices: Map real infrastructure to your configuration
items.explain: State is the mapping Terraform uses to plan diffs. Lose it and Terraform can no longer tell what is deployed.

choices: ReplicaSets, giving declarative updates and rollbacks for pods
items.explain: Deployments own ReplicaSets which own pods: the declarative path to rolling updates, scaling, and rollbacks.

choices: Every change ships a new image; servers are replaced, not patched in place
items.explain: Replace, don't patch: a fresh artifact per change makes deployments reproducible and rollbacks trivial.

items.q: Tests pass in the pipeline but production breaks. The best first response is…
choices: Check what differs between pipeline and prod: config, data, traffic
items.explain: Structured diagnosis starts with environment deltas — config, secrets, data, scale — before theorizing about code.

choices: The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it
Security is optional in the cloud
items.explain: Provider: physical hosts, hypervisor, facilities. You: data, IAM, configurations, workloads. The exam and the interview both test this line.

choices: Its route table has a route to an internet gateway
items.explain: Public means routable to the internet via an internet gateway; the route table entry is the mechanism.

items.q: Security groups vs NACLs: the key difference is…
choices: Security groups are stateful and instance-level; NACLs are stateless and subnet-level
items.explain: SGs remember return traffic (stateful) and attach to instances; NACLs evaluate every packet (stateless) at the subnet.

items.q: Object storage is best suited for…
choices: Blobs: images, backups, logs, static assets
items.explain: Object storage is durable, cheap blob storage — not a database, not a cache, not a filesystem.

items.q: A multi-AZ deployment primarily buys you…
choices: Resilience to a single datacenter failure
items.explain: Availability zones are isolated failure domains; spanning them survives a facility-level event.

items.q: The cheapest first step to cut a surprise cloud bill is…
choices: Tag resources, find idle ones, right-size them
items.explain: Visibility first: tag, find idle spend in the cost explorer, right-size. Commitments come after you know the shape of usage.

items.q: Parameterized queries defeat SQL injection because…
choices: User input is bound as data, never concatenated into SQL text
items.explain: Separating code from data: the input can never be parsed as SQL, no matter what it contains.

choices: In transit: confidentiality and integrity between client and server
items.explain: TLS encrypts the channel. It does nothing for data at rest or for application-layer bugs.

choices: A slow salted hash like bcrypt or Argon2
items.explain: Slow, salted, memory-hard hashing resists offline cracking. Plaintext, encoding, and fast hashes are breaches waiting to happen.

choices: The server can be tricked into requesting internal resources the attacker cannot reach
items.explain: Server-side request forgery turns your server's trusted network position against internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.

choices: A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques mapped to the attack lifecycle
items.explain: ATT&CK catalogs how attackers operate — the map defenders use for detection engineering and gap analysis.

choices: Each identity gets only the permissions its task requires
One shared account for the team
items.explain: Minimizing standing permissions shrinks the blast radius of any single compromise.

items.q: Two pointers is the right first thought when…
choices: The input is sorted or you need pairs satisfying a condition
You need to sort first anyway
items.explain: Sorted arrays and pair-sum conditions are two-pointer home turf: O(1) extra space with a clean narration.

items.q: In a system-design interview, you should start with…
choices: Requirements: functional, non-functional, and scale estimates
items.explain: Scope first: what the system must do and at what scale. Design without scale targets is guessing.

items.q: Back-of-envelope math in design interviews exists to…
choices: Size the system — QPS, storage, bandwidth — so choices are data-driven
items.explain: Numbers turn 'use a cache' into 'we need roughly X GB of cache for Y QPS': justified architecture.

choices: State the measurable outcome and what you learned
items.explain: Results with numbers prove impact; the reflection proves growth. Interviewers score both.

items.q: When you blank on a DSA problem, the best move is to…
choices: State the brute force, analyze it, then optimize aloud
items.explain: Brute-force-first shows process; narrated optimization shows thinking. Silence shows neither.

items.q: For 'design a URL shortener,' the core tradeoff discussion is…
choices: Read-heavy workload: caching, key generation, and storage for lookups
items.explain: Shorteners are read-dominated: the interview is really about cache strategy, ID generation, and storage at scale.
